signals.title: Inkling 2 Mini on vLLM: Day-0 Support for a Looped Model | vLLM Blog
signals.excerpt:
Thinking Machines announced Inkling 2 Mini today. vLLM supports it and its variable-loop research checkpoint, TML-d24-varloop-research, on day 0 on NVIDIA Blackwell, Hopper and DGX Spark. Inkling 2 Mini is a looped model: its middle 12 layers run three times per token with shared weights, each pass with its own KV cache and gated messages from the pass before. It is a multimodal MoE with 26B total and 3.5B active parameters, up to 1M tokens of context and a native DSpark speculator.

## TL;DR

- Looped layers. Layers 6–17 run three passes with shared weights. Each pass keeps its own KV cache and reads gated messages from the one before.
- 26B total, 3.5B active, 1M context, Native DSpark. A multimodal MoE built from Inkling 2 Small's components, with NVFP4 experts (MXFP8 in the last 4 layers) and a native DSpark speculator.
- Optimized day-0 support on Blackwell, Hopper and DGX Spark. vLLM manages each pass's caches like any other cache layer, fuses the message reads and controllers, and reuses Inkling 2 Small's fused kernels.
- RL support. vLLM serves Inkling 2 Mini for reinforcement learning with SkyRL.
- Variable-loop research checkpoint. vLLM also serves TML-d24-varloop-research, where you choose the number of passes, and whether the passes share one KV cache, at startup.

...

## Serving the Loop in vLLM

Per-pass caches as regular cache layers. vLLM registers each extra pass of a core layer as its own attention layer with its own KV and conv-state cache. The KV cache manager and prefix caching treat these caches like any others, so serving the loop needed no new cache-management logic.

Fused message reads and controllers. A direct implementation launches 4 message reads and 4 controllers, several kernels each, for every core layer in a later pass. vLLM reads all four messages of a layer in one attention-residual kernel and stacks the four controllers' weights, so their down and gain/forget projections run as batched GEMMs. One Triton kernel computes the controllers' RMS normalizations, and another fuses the gated merge with the RMSNorm of the sublayer the message feeds. The merge runs in FP32 without FMA contraction, matching the reference.

Fused kernels around every sublayer. For Inkling 2 Small, vLLM fuses each sublayer's all-reduce, short convolution, residual update, attention-residual mix and RMSNorm into one kernel. vLLM generalizes these kernels from hidden size 4,608 to 2,304 and adds a mode that returns the FP32 mix before the RMSNorm, so the later passes can merge their messages into it. Inkling 2 Mini uses them at every tensor-parallel size, including TP1; at TP > 1, small batches also fuse the all-reduce over NVLink multicast.

## Variable-Loop Research Checkpoint

Thinking Machines also releases TML-d24-varloop-research, a research checkpoint trained to run with a variable number of passes. vLLM exposes its two options through `--hf-overrides`:

...

- `loop_num_passes` sets the number of passes (at least 1; the default is the checkpoint's 3). Fewer passes are faster; more passes give higher quality. DSpark requires the default, since the draft reads fixed layer visits.
- `loop_share_cache` makes all passes of a core layer share one KV cache: each pass overwrites the keys and values of its tokens, so later tokens read the last pass's. Conv states stay per pass.

Both options are rejected on fixed-loop checkpoints such as Inkling 2 Mini. On one GB200 (TP1, 4K context, forward pass only):

| Passes | Decode step, batch 1 | Decode step, batch 32 | KV cache capacity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 1.51 ms | 3.81 ms | 352K tokens |
| 2 | 2.67 ms | 5.92 ms | 233K tokens |
| 3 | 3.85 ms | 8.11 ms | 175K tokens |
| 3, shared KV cache | 3.86 ms | 8.10 ms | 194K tokens |

Sharing the KV cache frees less memory than dropping a pass, because the per-pass conv-state caches remain.

## Accuracy Evals

vLLM keeps the reference implementation's numerics: the same data types at every step, the same NVFP4 and MXFP8 activation quantization, and FP32 message merges, with only the reduction order differing. On a fixed prompt, vLLM's hidden state at each of the 48 layer visits differs from the reference by about as much as the reference's own FlashAttention-4 and PyTorch attention paths differ from each other, and the MoE outputs match bitwise given the same inputs.

End to end, we tested accuracy on needle-in-a-haystack up to 1M tokens, MMMU-Pro and HLE with inkling-verify, and on GSM8K, with DSpark enabled.

signals.title: Cut self-hosted LLM cost and latency with the distributed KV caching agent skill | Artificial Intelligence
signals.excerpt:
by Ravi Yadav, Chaitanya Nuthalapati, and Neeraj Ramachandran on 20 NOV 2026 in Amazon ElastiCache, Expert (400), Technical How-to Permalink Share

Customers increasingly self-host large language models (LLMs) on GPUs for control over cost, accuracy, and latency. However, self-hosting often means paying for redundant GPU work because small, isolated caches on each server can’t hold or share the growing context AI agents and chat applications resend. Consider a legal AI assistant that can accumulate hundreds of thousands of tokens of case history in each conversation. When a lawyer returns to a thread after lunch, responses from the LLM can take minutes. The GPU server that picks up the request has none of that history in its memory. So, the GPU recomputes the key-value (KV) attention states for all of those tokens, a step called prefill, before it writes a word. The same pattern slows down resumed coding agents, agentic AI assistants, and document Q&A assistants. Distributed KV caching with Amazon ElastiCache can cut self-hosted LLM inference costs by up to 40% and time to first token (TTFT) by up to 80%. Distributed KV caching extends GPU-local caches with a shared tier beside your GPU fleet so any server can reuse KV state for days across sessions, routing shifts, and server failures. “ Announcing distributed KV caching for self-hosted LLMs with Amazon ElastiCache” dives into the technical details and the performance benchmarks.

This post details the distributed KV caching skill in the Agent Toolkit for AWS. With this skill, you can evaluate and set up distributed KV caching from within your coding agent in a few prompts. The skill guides the agent through checking whether your workload benefits from distributed KV caching, setting up a cache cluster for testing or production workload, and troubleshooting your LLM inference caching. The skill works with Kiro, Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and other coding agents that support Agent Skills. We walk through how the skill works with four conversations: diagnosing a slow first token, sizing and pricing the cache, setting it up, and fixing a failed transfer.

## Why a skill for KV caching and what can it do?

The benefits for your workload depend on characteristics such as LLM models used, user traffic patterns, and prompt routing choices, and can be complex to estimate. We created the KVTrace tool to get close estimates of the benefits for your workload, from your own model and traffic before you deploy any infrastructure, at no additional charge. The skill simplifies this evaluation and the setup, and guides your coding agent through the following best practices before changing anything:

- A fit check before any spend. The agent reads your GPU fleet with a read-only `describe-instances` call and counts Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) interfaces. It asks only for what it can’t see: engine, model, tensor-parallel (TP) size, KV data type, server price, and how often prompts repeat. It stops and explains when something doesn’t fit.
- Numbers from your workload. For short prompts, loading KV state can take longer than computing it again. Above a certain prompt length (the cutover point), the read wins. That cutover and how often your prompts repeat decide whether the cache is worth its price. The agent estimates savings from your own traffic with KVTrace, at no additional charge, and stops if they don’t cover the cache’s cost. Every number says where it came from.
- Manage configuration across inference servers with the stack you already run. The agent adds the LMCache connector to your existing vLLM or SGLang engine, including vLLM workers under serving frameworks such as llm-d and Ray Serve. It keeps your routing and the engine’s settings and sets the servers in your inference fleet to one KV ID mechanism (hash and seed) and an explicit KV data type. Matching settings avoid key mismatches, where each server writes KV state the others can’t find.
- Implements best practices. Before production traffic, the agent empties the local tiers and checks that two cache-loaded runs give the same output, because a layout mismatch can produce healthy hit counters and wrong answers. The skill guides the agent to seek explicit approval for high-impact operations such as creating, changing, or deleting resources.

## Prerequisites

These flows, from estimating benefits to setup, require the following:

- A coding agent that supports Agent Skills, such as Kiro or Claude Code.
- GPU instances that support EFA RDMA write, such as p5.
- LMCache 0.5.8rc1 or later and vLLM 0.11.1 or later (SGLang 0.5.13 or later).
- ElastiCache for Valkey 9.1 or later, on cache.i8ge.48xlarge nodes (if setting up the cache).

...

To size the savings, we gave the agent an example fleet of 8 p5 instances that serve 64,000-token prompts for a multi-turn retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) assistant.

signals.title: Skip the DRAM Tier: MoRI UMBP Runs the Agentic KV Cache on NVMe | vLLM Blog
signals.excerpt:
Most of the traffic in agentic serving is multi-turn sessions that resend long prefixes. In the AgentX benchmark replaying real Claude Code sessions, the median turn is 142K input tokens, and over 96% of those tokens are a prefix the server has already seen [3].

A KV cache hit means the prefill node only has to process the small delta. A miss forces a full recomputation of the prefix, which burns GPU time and delays the first token. In our 42 runs of Kimi-K3 on vLLM, raising the KV cache hit rate by 1% of prompt tokens, for example from 95% to 96%, was worth about 10% more throughput (Figure 3).

A KV cache hit needs the session’s prefix to still be in memory when its next turn arrives. With dozens of sessions open at once, memory runs out. GPU memory goes first, and host DRAM is the usual next tier. But DRAM fills too: Kimi-K3 wrote 2.3 to 4.6 TB of KV to the pool an hour in our runs, so a 1.8 TB DRAM pool, which lists at about $76,000, holds only the last 23 to 47 minutes of it.

That led us to a simple question: why not skip the DRAM tier and put vLLM’s KV pool straight on NVMe? We tried it on AMD Instinct™ MI355X GPUs with UMBP, the KV cache pool in AMD’s open-source MoRI library. At the same size, NVMe matched DRAM’s throughput within 1% on Kimi-K3, in two sets of runs on different machines (Figure 1). On a second workload with longer prompts, NVMe came within 1% of a DRAM pool of the same size. The NVMe pool has no DRAM tier: DRAM only buffers new KV on its way to the drives and stages reads, about 80 GB against the DRAM pool’s 1.8 TB.

...

On vLLM, a 1.8 TB NVMe KV pool matched a 1.8 TB DRAM pool: Kimi-K3’s throughput stayed within ... On longer prompts, NVMe came within 1% of a DRAM pool of the same size at 70 sessions.
- No DRAM tier. All 1.8 TB of the KV pool is on NVMe. DRAM only buffers the last minute or two of writes (64 GB) and stages reads from the drives (16 GiB): about 80 GB, under 5% of the pool. At 70 sessions the pool also ran without the write buffer at no cost; under heavier load, keep it.
- Why. Throughput follows the KV cache hit rate, and same-size pools that evict the same way keep the same KV. vLLM loads KV asynchronously, so on a busy engine NVMe’s slower load finished while the request waited for prefill.
- What NVMe buys. Retention. DRAM costs per TB held; NVMe costs per TB written. At list prices, drives rated for Kimi-K3’s 83 TB of writes a day hold a day of KV for about $59,000; a $76,000 DRAM pool holds 31 minutes.
- Limitation and roadmap. Every block of KV the GPU computes is written to the drives, wearing them out, so we will spread those writes over more SSDs with a distributed version of the pool.

signals.title: New benchmark tests AI agents on building RAG — Grafy News
signals.excerpt:
Researchers have introduced AutoRAGBench to evaluate how well AI agents can autonomously design and refine RAG pipelines in open coding environments.

Grafy News Desk Nov 20, 2026 5 min read

Source: Grafy Research Lab

Researchers have introduced AutoRAGBench, a new benchmark designed to evaluate the ability of Large Language Model (LLM) agents to autonomously develop Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems. This development matters because while RAG is a standard method for grounding AI answers in external data, building an effective pipeline currently requires significant manual engineering and constant iterative testing by human developers.

## What is AutoRAGBench and how does it work?

According to the researchers, AutoRAGBench is the first benchmark to assess how well AI agents can build RAG systems from scratch within an open code space. Unlike previous evaluations that focus on how well a specific RAG configuration performs, this benchmark measures the agent's ability to act as a developer.

In the experimental setup, agents are given a task involving specific corpora—covering domains like medicine and news—and are tasked with building a RAG pipeline. They are provided with a six-hour time limit and a single H800 GPU. Within this isolated environment, agents must write their own code, install necessary libraries, and download auxiliary models to solve the task. The benchmark includes nine distinct development tasks to ensure the agents are tested across various requirements, such as multi-hop reasoning or fact verification.

## How well can AI agents automate RAG development?

The study evaluated nine different agent configurations. The results indicated that agents are capable of automating effective RAG development. Specifically, the researchers found that the GPT-6.1 Sol configuration using Codex CLI achieved the highest average score of 56.1 points. This performance exceeded the composite Human-SOTA (State-of-the-Art) baseline, which averaged 44.4 points under the same protocol.

Furthermore, the researchers noted that these agents do not just build static systems; they can improve upon existing ones. When the agents were given human-designed systems to work with across seven different tasks, they improved the scores by an average of 16.6 points. They achieved these gains while maintaining the core mechanisms of the original human-designed methods, suggesting that agents can refine and optimize rather than simply replacing logic with random configurations.

## How is the performance of these agents measured?

To ensure a rigorous evaluation, the researchers employed a two-part assessment: RAG system evaluation and development process evaluation.

For the system evaluation, the researchers used five different held-out answering models to test the accuracy of the retrieved evidence. By averaging the scores across these models, they could isolate the quality of the RAG system itself from the potential biases of a single answering model.

For the development process, the researchers analyzed the "trajectories" of the agents. This involved looking at how the agents prepared for a task, how they implemented their retrieval methods, and how they used experimental feedback to guide their revisions. This allowed the team to see if the agents were actually learning from their mistakes or simply iterating blindly. The researchers observed that in 72 out of 77 builds with comparable scores, the agents reached a final version that was at least one point higher than their initial attempt.

## What are the limitations of automated RAG development?

While the results are promising, the researchers identified certain complexities in the development cycle. They noted that larger gains during the development phase do not always translate to higher accuracy on hidden test sets. Additionally, the study found that in 20 builds, the final observed development score was at least one point lower than the best score achieved during the process, indicating that agents can sometimes regress during iteration.

This highlights the difficulty of the task: choosing the right retrieval strategy, context construction, and evidence selection is highly dependent on the specific corpus and the types of questions being asked. The ability of an agent to navigate these design choices autonomously is the primary frontier being tested by AutoRAGBench.

...

Source: Hang Zhang et al., AutoRAGBench: A Benchmark for LLM Agents Automating RAG System Development (arXiv:2611.2558)

signals.title: Saturn Cloud Brings Tileward's Compressed Models to Its Token Factory, Turning the Same GPUs Into More Tokens
signals.excerpt:
Nov 20, 2026, 13:00 ET

Tileward's compressed open models free up GPU memory, so operators on Saturn Cloud's token factory platform can serve more tokens from the GPUs they already own, with no change to their serving stack or rate cards.

NEW YORK, Nov. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Saturn Cloud, the inference platform for enterprises running open models, today announced a partnership with Tileward to bring its compressed open models to Saturn Cloud's token factory platform. Operators can run the same models with less GPU memory, so each GPU can serve more tokens.

Saturn Cloud's token factory turns GPU fleets into managed inference and fine-tuning services that operators sell to their own customers, under their own brand. Tenant isolation, quotas, metering, and enterprise governance are built in. It runs on NVIDIA Dynamo, in public cloud, private cloud, or on-premises. Serving Kimi K3 to 16 live agent sessions on NVIDIA GB300 GPUs, Saturn Cloud delivered 7,380 total tokens per second per GPU at about 37 tokens per second per user, matching the SemiAnalysis InferenceX benchmark recipe on the same GPUs. Tileward's models run on this serving stack.

"Operators sell inference from GPUs they've already paid for, and memory is usually what runs out first," said Sebastian Metti, Founder and CEO of Saturn Cloud. "Tileward gives that memory back, so operators can take on more customers and longer contexts with the fleet they have, without buying more GPUs."

Tileward, a member of the NVIDIA Inception program for startups, offers compressed models that are up to 78% smaller than the published weights. Tileward evaluates each one against the original on benchmarks including MMLU, SWE-bench Verified, and AgentBench.

"Making a model smaller was never the hard part. Proving it still gives the right answers is," said Anantha Sharma, Founder and CTO of Tileward. "We publish how we measure every model, so operators on Saturn Cloud can check the quality before they sell a single token of it."

Operators can swap in Tileward's weights for the published ones, and their serving stack, tenants, rate cards, and brand stay the same. The freed memory lets them run more copies of each model, fit large models on fewer GPUs, and serve more concurrent users with longer contexts. Serving more tokens from each GPU lowers the cost per token, giving operators more margin on input, cached, and output rates, or room to price lower.

Available Now on Saturn Cloud

Compressed versions of gpt-oss-120b, GLM-5.3, and DeepSeek-V4-Flash are available now to neoclouds, AI factory operators, telcos, sovereign AI providers, and enterprises running Saturn Cloud's token factory platform on their own GPUs. Contact Saturn Cloud or Tileward to add them to a deployment.

signals.title: Amazon SageMaker JumpStart now offers a model leaderboard to compare models on quality, speed, and cost - AWS
signals.excerpt:
Posted on: Nov 20, 2026 

Amazon SageMaker JumpStart now offers a model leaderboard in Amazon SageMaker Studio. You can use it to compare foundation models side by side on throughput, latency, and cost, and then deploy or customize the model that fits your workload.

Comparing models has usually meant reading model cards one at a time and relying on benchmark scores that different sources published under different conditions. The JumpStart leaderboard puts consistent measurements in one view. AWS evaluates every model on three reasoning benchmarks, BIG-Bench Hard, GPQA Diamond, and MMLU-Pro, using the same evaluation setup for each model. AWS also measures time to first token, throughput, and instance cost on SageMaker for each JumpStart deployment configuration. You can use all of the filters already available for JumpStart models, such as model provider, license, and input and output modality, to narrow the list. You can also choose a use case profile and an optimization goal (balanced, cost, latency, or throughput) to see the metrics for the configuration you plan to deploy. At launch, the leaderboard covers more than 70 LLMs from providers including Meta, Google, Qwen, IBM, and Arcee.

The JumpStart model leaderboard is available at no additional charge in all AWS commercial Regions where Amazon SageMaker Studio is available. To get started, open SageMaker JumpStart in SageMaker Studio and choose the Leaderboard view. To learn more, see JumpStart leaderboard methodology and read the launch blog post.

signals.title: Meta TLX Brings Warp-Group GPU Control to Triton on Hopper, Blackwell, AMD - MarkTechPost
signals.excerpt:
Meta has published a detailed report on TLX (Triton Low-Level Extensions). It is the GPU compiler extension behind Meta’s production ML kernels. Meta TLX is a Triton extension that exposes warp groups, barriers, TMA and clusters to Python kernels. It targets NVIDIA Hopper and Blackwell plus AMD MI300 and MI350-series GPUs. For kernel engineers, the message is CUDA-level control without leaving Triton.

## TL;DR

- What it is: an extension to Triton, not a new language. A Blackwell GEMM takes roughly 200 lines of Python-level Triton.
- Runs on: NVIDIA Hopper (H100) and Blackwell (B200, GB200), AMD MI300 and MI350-series. MIT-licensed.
- Performance: within -0.9% to +3.7% of cuBLAS on 6 H100 FP16 GEMM shapes (PyTorch).
- Best: a 4x speedup on an H100 linear compression kernel for ads inference (Meta).
- Worst: dense LLM-style attention forward reaches about 87% of FlashAttention-4 on B200 (PyTorch).
- Bottom line: Best: hand-tuned performance from short Triton code. Worst: all numbers are self-reported, with no independent benchmarks yet.

...

## How fast is TLX? Benchmarks

All figures below are self-reported by Meta:

- H100 GEMM: across 6 FP16 shapes, TLX lands between -0.9% and +3.7% of cuBLAS. On 8192x8192x8192 it reaches 577.0 TFLOPS versus 582.3 for cuBLAS (PyTorch).
- MI350 GEMM: TLX beats rocBLAS by 11.8% to 15.2% on square shapes from 256 to 2048.
- B200 attention: On production jagged shapes, Meta’s Jagged Flash Attention beats FlashAttention-4 by about 13% forward. Backward runs about 50% faster. On dense LLM-style shapes, forward reaches about 87% of FA4 (PyTorch).
- Code size: that attention kernel is about 3.2K lines. Meta estimates FA4 at 10K lines of CuTe DSL.

The research team adds that TLX trails state-of-the-art attention most on the smallest causal-forward cases. The gap narrows as sequence length grows.

## Where is TLX used in production at Meta?

Meta’s engineering post lists 3 case studies:

- Generative Ads Model (GEM) training: 20% to 25% end-to-end MFU on thousands of GPUs. TLX delivered up to 2x forward speedup for Generalized Dot Product Attention.
- In-Kernel Broadcast Optimization (IKBO): a warp-specialized linear compression kernel hit 4x speedup on H100. FlashAttention under IKBO cut compute-intensive net latency by up to two-thirds.
- Distributed grouped GEMM: fuses mixture-of-experts matmuls with communication for LLM pretraining on Blackwell. Meta gives no speedup figure.

Meta also compared CUTLASS, CuTe DSL and TLX on Blackwell for GEM. It says TLX gave the best productivity-performance balance for most kernels, but shares no numbers.

...

TLX lives in Meta’s MIT-licensed Triton fork, facebookexperimental/triton, under `third_party/tlx/`. It also ships as `triton-utlx` on PyPI, a plugin for upstream Triton. The PyTorch-Triton 3.7 plugin system loads TLX without forking Triton. AMD has also published a GEMM plus activation guide for CDNA4 with TLX.

이번에 공개된 릴레이트는 급증하는 에이전트 워크로드(데이터 처리 작업량)에 맞춰 설계된 초고속 인메모리(데이터를 주기억장치인 RAM에 올려 처리하는 방식) 데이터베이스로, 개발자들이 AI 에이전트를 위한 애플리케이션을 밀리초(ms, 1초의 1천분의 1) 단위로 구축할 수 있도록 지원합니다.

## 러스트 기반 구조와 서브 밀리초 단위의 고성능 실행

릴레이트는 시스템 프로그래밍 언어인 러스트(Rust, 메모리 안정성과 빠른 실행 속도를 제공하는 프로그래밍 언어)로 처음부터 새롭게 구축되었습니다. 이를 통해 자율 에이전트의 고빈도 읽기 및 쓰기 주기에 대응할 수 있는 서브 밀리초(0밀리초 미만) 수준의 읽기 속도를 제공합니다.

- 인프로세스 및 인메모리 작동: 별도의 데이터베이스 서버를 거치지 않고 에이전트 프로세스 내부에서 직접 실행되어 지연 시간을 최소화합니다.
- 영구 저장 지원: 가벼운 인메모리 저장소로 작동하는 동시에, 필요할 때 디스크에 상태를 기록할 수 있는 쓰기 선행 로그(WAL, Write-Ahead Log, 데이터 변경 사항을 디스크에 미리 기록해 장애 복구를 돕는 기록 장치)와 파일 동기화 옵션을 제공하여 데이터의 신뢰성을 보장합니다.
- 표준 쿼리 지원: 100% 오픈시퍼(openCypher, 그래프 데이터베이스 질의 언어 표준) 및 97% 이상의 GQL(Graph Query Language, 그래프 질의 언어 국제 표준) 호환성을 갖추고 있습니다.

## AI 에이전트를 위한 네이티브 통합 기능

최근 엔터프라이즈 환경에서는 단순한 질의응답을 넘어 여러 단계를 스스로 계획하고 실행하는 다단계 자율 에이전트 도입이 빠르게 늘고 있습니다. 가트너의 전망에 따르면 기계 사용자(AI 에이전트)의 데이터베이스 워크로드 비중은 2025년 10%에서 2029년 75%까지 급증할 것으로 예상됩니다. 릴레이트는 이러한 에이전트 중심 패러다임에 맞춰 설계되었습니다.

- 멀티홉 추론 및 GraphRAG: 여러 단계의 연관 관계를 탐색하는 멀티홉(Multi-hop) 추론과 지식 그래프를 활용해 LLM의 환각 현상을 줄이고 정확도를 높이는 GraphRAG(그래프 기반 검색 증강 생성) 기능을 제공합니다.
- 자동 에이전트 하네스 감지: 에이전트가 실행되는 환경을 자동으로 감지하며, 예외 상황 발생 시 명시적인 재시도(Retryable) 플래그가 포함된 구조화된 에러를 반환해 에이전트가 스스로 오류를 수정할 수 있도록 돕습니다.
- 컨텍스트 윈도우 보호: 대규모 데이터 검색 시 컨텍스트 윈도우(LLM이 한 번에 처리할 수 있는 최대 토큰 크기)가 포화되는 것을 막기 위해 행 수 상한(Row Cap)과 인밴드 잘라내기 마커를 적용하여 예측 가능한 크기의 데이터만 에이전트에 전달합니다.

## 현대적인 AI 스택과의 간편한 연동 및 가용성

릴레이트는 주피터 노트북(Jupyter Notebook, 데이터 분석 및 코드 실행을 지원하는 웹 기반 대화형 환경), 웹 브라우저, 소프트웨어 컨테이너(Container, 프로그램 실행 환경을 격리해주는 가상화 기술), 에지 기기 등 에이전트가 활동하는 모든 곳에서 유연하게 배포됩니다.

- 기본 연동 인터페이스: 모델 맥락 프로토콜(MCP, Model Context Protocol, AI 모델과 외부 데이터소스 간의 상 호작용을 표준화한 프로토콜) 서버와 전용 명령줄 인터페이스(CLI, Command Line Interface)를 기본 내장하고 있습니다.
- 표준 엔드포인트: Bolt 및 HTTP Query API v2 엔드포인트를 제공하여 기존의 그래프 드라이버, 오케스트레이션 프레임워크(에이전트의 작업 흐름을 조율하는 도구), 개발자 도구와 바로 연동할 수 있습니다.

릴레이트는 아파치 2.0(Apache 2.0) 라이선스 하에 오픈소스로 제공되며, 공식 웹사이트를 통해 설치 및 활용을 시작할 수 있습니다. 네오4J는 이를 통해 개발자들이 에이전트 메모리와 샌드박스 환경에서 고성능 그래프 데이터 처리를 손쉽게 구현할 수 있을 것으로 기대하고 있습니다.

signals.title: FlashInfer on ROCm routes AMD GPU kernels automatically | AI.info
signals.excerpt:
FlashInfer on ROCm now selects between AMD's AITER library and in-tree HIP kernels for supported attention calls, using a default automatic backend. The release, described in an AMD blog post on November 20, also adds FP8 prefill, fused mixture-of-experts operations and AITER decode under CUDA graph capture.

FlashInfer is an open-source library of attention and large language model serving kernels. The ROCm release supports AMD Instinct MI300X, MI325X, MI350X and MI355X GPUs. Its decode, prefill and multi-head latent attention (MLA) wrappers retain the signatures and argument order of upstream FlashInfer v0.6.18.

## How routing works

Single, batch paged and batch ragged prefill, as well as batch decode, have both AITER and in-tree HIP backends. For attention calls, the automatic setting first checks whether AITER can handle the data types, key-value cache layout, masks and head dimensions, then applies architecture-specific routing rules.

AMD says those rules follow its testing and benchmarking on CDNA3 and CDNA4 GPUs. The in-tree path handles calls that AITER cannot serve, including an FP8 key-value cache read by a 16-bit query and batch decode using tensor cores.

MLA and fused mixture-of-experts operations use AITER only. Normalization, activation, rotary position embedding and key-value cache append operations use in-tree kernels by default, with AITER available as an opt-in for some entry points.

After planning a batch prefill or batch decode call, the wrapper reports the selected backend and, for most AITER declines, the reason for the fallback. AITER attention kernels are launched from FlashInfer's C++ code; MLA remains an exception that runs AITER through Python.

## New operations and limits

The release also brings cascade attention, MLA and standalone rotary position embedding operations that were in progress in the preceding prefill-attention release. POD-Attention overlaps prefill and decode in one kernel.

The fused mixture-of-experts operation supports bf16 and fp16, as well as FP8 expert weights. Each expert weight must first be pre-shuffled, following quantization for FP8 weights.

The in-tree FP8 key-value cache kernels use FNUZ encodings on both supported architectures and refuse OCP encodings. On gfx950, a cache written in float8_e4m3fn for AITER FP8 prefill cannot also be read by decode: the in-tree decode rejects that encoding, while AITER decode accepts only 16-bit key-value caches.

Some upstream modules are not supported on ROCm because they wrap CUDA-only libraries or other CUDA-specific components. Other operations, including flashinfer.topk and the selective state update in flashinfer.mamba, do not have a ROCm implementation.

## Building and compiling

The supported configuration uses ROCm 10.1.0, PyTorch 2.12.0, Python 3.12, Ubuntu 24.04 and amd-aiter 0.1.21.post2 built from source. No wheel or prebuilt image is published for the release, so FlashInfer on ROCm must be built from the repository.

Selected attention, cache-append and fused mixture-of-experts operations can compile under torch.compile when the custom-operations flag is set before importing FlashInfer. AMD cautions that PyTorch 2.12 can silently miscompile an operation that writes into a view of a larger tensor, and specifies separately allocated key and value caches for append_paged_kv_cache.

signals.title: Can AI help scientists identify promising drug candidates? | OpenAI
signals.excerpt:
We’re introducing MedChemBench, a benchmark that evaluates AI models on reasoning tasks drawn from medicinal chemistry research. It tests whether models can connect a molecule’s structure with experimental evidence to explain results, compare compounds, and predict their properties. Building AI that can reliably support this work is one step towards helping scientists develop better medicines.

...

MedChemBench measures these abilities through 99 problems drawn from published research. At the xhigh reasoning setting, GPT‑6.2 Astra earned 84.5% of the available credit, compared with 83.3% for GPT‑6 Astra, 82.0% for GPT‑6.1 Sol, and 58.2% for GPT‑5.6 Sol. GPT‑6 Astra was strongest at reconstructing molecular structures and explaining experimental evidence. Selecting compounds and predicting their numerical properties proved harder for that model.

## What MedChemBench grades

MedChemBench draws on 117 papers and patents and includes 761 distinct molecular structures. For most problems, models receive the context available at a chosen point in a research program: the biological target, the researchers’ goals, the compounds studied so far, and selected experimental findings.

The benchmark evaluates four components:

- Molecular structures. Correct atom connections and specified stereochemistry in molecules assembled from the drawings and chemical groups provided.
- Scientific reasoning. Explanations supported by the supplied evidence, such as the reasons for choosing one compound over another.
- Ranking and selection. Compound rankings and choices that meet the stated requirements.
- Property predictions. Agreement with the numerical values and categories reported in the source material, including measured and calculated molecular properties.

signals.title: Tencent's Hy4 runs on MetaX's Chinese GPU with FlagOS W8A8 | iMasters
signals.excerpt:
MetaX says its C550 GPUs already support Tencent's flagship Hy4 model (Hunyuan), released on November 20, and published a quantized version via FlagOS.

...

## What MetaX announced

Chinese GPU maker MetaX says it completed a "day-zero" adaptation of its C-series GPUs to Hy4, Tencent's flagship model, hours after the company released the model's weights for download on November 20, 2026. Alongside this, MetaX published a W8A8 quantized version of Hy4 built on FlagOS, according to a Pandaily report published on November 22.

It's important to separate two things the news bundles together. One is the hardware and software adaptation to run the original Hy4 on MetaX's C550 GPUs. The other is this W8A8 version, which is not a new model trained from scratch: it's a lighter way of serving the same weights, using eight bits for weights and activations instead of the original precision. Pandaily also notes that this release is separate from MetaX's earlier adaptation to "Hy4 flash" (a leaner variant of the same model) and from Tencent's original announcement, covered in another Pandaily report.

## MXMACA and FlagOS: the stack trying to play CUDA's role

MetaX attributes the quick integration to its MXMACA software stack, which includes drivers, interfaces, the MXCC compiler, operator adaptation, and connections to inference frameworks. In practice, it's an attempt to offer Chinese GPUs the same kind of layer that CUDA offers Nvidia GPUs: without it, running a large model on different hardware requires rewriting operator by operator.

FlagOS, behind the W8A8 version, is a BAAI (Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence) project to standardize operators across different Chinese chips. Pandaily published another piece on FlagOS version 2.2, which already covers 1,454 operators across manufacturers such as MetaX and Huawei Ascend. The stated goal is to let the same quantized model run on multiple domestic accelerators without manual rewriting, which matters in a market where access to cutting-edge Nvidia GPUs remains restricted by US export controls.

## The 32-GPU benchmark: throughput rises, initial latency gets worse

The model card accompanying the release describes a cluster of four servers, each with eight 64GB C550 GPUs, totaling 32 GPUs. The test uses 64 concurrent requests, with roughly 4,000 input tokens and 1,000 output tokens per request, according to the report. These specific hardware and load conditions matter for interpreting the numbers, because they are not equivalent to a production test with real traffic.

| Metric | With decode-graph | Without decode-graph |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Aggregate output throughput | 80.98 tokens/s | 52.31 tokens/s |
| Average time to first token (with queue) | 227.2 s | 220.5 s |

In other words: the "decode-graph" mode recommended by MetaX increases throughput by about 55%, but time to first token got worse, not better, when the waiting queue is counted in. Both numbers come from the same card and the same report, and together they rule out any reading that "everything improved": there is a real trade-off between aggregate throughput and latency perceived per individual request.

Two additional points limit the benchmark's scope. The deployment recipe uses a maximum context of 65,536 tokens, well below the 1 million token capacity Tencent advertises for the original Hy4, so the numbers say nothing about long-context performance. The card also marks two multimodal evaluations as "in progress," not completed.

In short: the numbers come from the manufacturer itself, specific to one configuration, and Pandaily was explicit in treating them as "vendor claims," not as independently verified results in real applications.

## What Pandaily's verification found (and didn't find)

It's worth highlighting a reporting detail that sets this coverage apart from a simple reproduced press release. The cited FlagRelease repository is public and contains weight files in safetensors format available for download, not just an announcement or a hosted demo. In the verification, a limited request managed to retrieve 64 bytes from a weight fragment listed in the repository.

Pandaily did not download the complete model or run the deployment described in the card. This means the existence of the weights was confirmed, but the performance MetaX declared was not independently reproduced.

signals.title: Google adds Tool Retrieval to let AI agents manage hundreds of tools
signals.excerpt:
Google has introduced Tool Retrieval, a new preview feature in the Gemini API that lets artificial intelligence agents tap into hundreds of software tools without loading every tool’s full definition into each request.

The feature, announced on the Google blog, is designed to cut input token usage and latency as developers build agents with increasingly large tool libraries.

## What the feature does

 Tool Retrieval is now in preview in the Gemini Interactions API , letting developers load tool parameter schemas on demand instead of sending their full tool library in every prompt.

It is designed to reduce input tokens and keep tool selection accurate as an agent scales. Google said when an agent connects to dozens or even hundreds of tools, sending every full parameter schema on every request adds up fast.

 Tool Retrieval lets your agent keep its full tool library on standby and load parameter schemas only when the current task needs them. 

 Developers can turn the feature on by adding a tool_search tool and setting defer_loading to true in their requests. Once that is configured, when the model needs a tool, it asks for it by name, the API loads the full schema, and the model calls the function , all inside the same request.

...

## Server and client options

Google is offering two ways to run the retrieval step. There is no index to build or host. Gemini runs the search on the server, so the only code changes are the new tool and a flag on the tools you defer. 

For companies that maintain their own systems, developers who maintain their own tool registry, embedding index or per-user permission filter can use client-side retrieval by declaring tool_search with “execution”: “client” and defining their search parameters.

That client-side option carries a tradeoff. Client-side retrieval adds one round trip per search, because your app runs the lookup. 

But the client-side option does not require tools to be declared upfront , so new tools can be exposed mid-conversation when a user connects an integration.

...

The capability is limited to Google’s newer model lineup, as Tool Retrieval works with Gemini 3.6 and later models, including all Gemini 4 models, in the Interactions API.

...

Google confirmed Tool Retrieval also works with remote MCP servers in the Gemini API , meaning agents connected to outside services through the Model Context Protocol can benefit from the same deferred loading approach.

Because the feature remains in preview, Google cautioned that it carries some risk. One outlet summarizing the documentation noted that any system that decides which tools to surface introduces its own failure mode: if the retrieval step misses the right tool, the model never gets a chance to pick it. 

Google has not stated when the feature will move to general availability.

signals.title: TensorRT-LLM V1.3.0 Brings NVFP4 To Hopper And Ada, Drops Legacy Backend | Smart Chunks
signals.excerpt:
## TL;DR

- NVIDIA’s TensorRT-LLM v1.3.0 adds MXFP8, an 8-bit number format, for standard layers and mixture-of-experts layers.
- A new 4-bit, weight-only NVFP4 path built on Marlin means NVFP4 checkpoints now run on Hopper and Ada Lovelace GPUs.
- NVFP4 quantization is now tunable, and PyTorch is the only backend left.
- The practical upshot: more NVIDIA GPUs can serve newer compressed models.

## Two new low-precision paths and one big deletion

Quantization means storing a model’s numbers with fewer bits. Fewer bits means a smaller memory footprint. NVIDIA’s TensorRT-LLM v1.3.0 release adds two new ways to do that.

The first is MXFP8, written as W8A8. That label means the weights (the numbers the model learned) and the activations (the values it computes while running) both use 8 bits. Support covers linear layers, the basic matrix-math blocks, and MoE layers. MoE is short for mixture of experts: a model split into specialist sub-networks, where only a few work on each token.

The release notes name MiniMax-M3 as one supported MXFP8 checkpoint. A checkpoint is simply a saved set of model weights. The exact line reads: “Added MXFP8 (W8A8) linear and MoE support, including MXFP8 checkpoints such as MiniMax-M3.”

The second path is the one I’d watch. NVIDIA “added W4A16 NVFP4 weight-only quantization through Marlin, so NVFP4 checkpoints run on Hopper and Ada Lovelace.” Translation: weights are stored in 4 bits while activations stay at 16. Marlin is a set of GPU kernels, the small programs that do the actual math. Hopper and Ada Lovelace are two NVIDIA GPU generations.

The release also adds tunable NVFP4 quantization. It supports both legacy and ModelOpt 1.x quantization config formats. The notes don’t spell out what “tunable” lets you adjust.

...

The release notes don’t say how much speed or memory you actually gain, so I won’t guess.

...

## The quieter change: PyTorch is now the only backend

TensorRT-LLM is NVIDIA’s open-source library for optimizing and serving large language models on its GPUs. A backend is the engine underneath that actually executes the model. Version 1.3.0 removes the legacy TensorRT backend, which leaves PyTorch as the sole backend.

signals.title: A free memory layer for your agents, and why you still don't know you need it - DEV Community
signals.excerpt:
Giulio D'Erme
Posted on Nov 20
# A free memory layer for your agents, and why you still don't know you need it
**No install needed to try it:** ask the beta chatbot on re-call.dev. It runs on RE-call.

...

In August my `CLAUDE.md` and `MEMORY.md` together held 17,499 characters. The memory folder behind them held 636,191, in 185 files. That is 36 to 1. Claude Code loads the first 200 lines of `MEMORY.md` at start-up. Most of what my agents had learned sat outside what they read.
RE-call is a memory layer for that work. It saves what agents learn, finds it the moment the work needs it, and abstains when it has nothing. Version 0.16.0 runs completely free.
## Two commands, zero spend
```
python -m pip install "recall-rag[fastembed,mcp]>=0.16.0"
recall setup --lite --memory ./notes
```
Point it at a folder of Markdown notes. Restart your agent. Ask it something your notes answer. It needs Python 3.11.5 or newer.
What you get:
* SQLite on your disk. No Docker, no database server.
* A local embedder (`BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5`). It downloads once, then runs on your CPU.
* No API key. No account.
* No LLM call to store a memory, build the graph or search.
* AGPL-3.0. All of it is on GitHub.
Your agent is the only LLM in the loop. The memory layer spends nothing.
## What runs under it
**Hybrid rank fusion.** Every search runs two ways: dense vectors and full-text search. Reciprocal rank fusion merges the two lists. The exact error code and the fuzzy description of a failure both find the same memo.
**Atomic rescue.** Sometimes the answer is one sentence buried in a long memo. RE-call cuts each chunk into short 24 word views and embeds them locally. When one view matches the query closely, its memo moves up. At most one memo, and only in rank. It can never turn an abstention into an answer. In 0.16.0 it is on from the first install.
**Semantic graph.** RE-call reads what your memos already state: links, `supersedes:`, `depends\_on`, headings. It builds a graph from them with no model. The dashboard draws it, so you can follow which memo replaced which.
**Trust layer.** It calibrates a threshold on your own store. Below it, search abstains instead of handing back the nearest note. A memo that declares `supersedes:` outranks the one it replaces. An expired memo comes back flagged. On Lite, `forget` zeroes the deleted bytes in the file.
Every search returns a verdict: trusted, degraded or abstained. With the reason.

...

Fewer errors
I measured it. Claude Code with Haiku 4.5, four trap tasks, 40 paired runs. Each fix lived only in memory, never in `CLAUDE.md`.
* `CLAUDE.md` alone: the agent fell into the trap 21 times in 40.
* The same `CLAUDE.md` plus RE-call: 0 times in 40.
One trap: onnxruntime ignores `OMP\_NUM\_THREADS`. Without memory, the agent fell for it 9 times in 10.

...

## Limits
Abstention works on far gaps. On near misses it often fails. The trap study used four traps and one model, on my PostgreSQL store rather than Lite. A separate task success study found no overall uplift. Every number and its limit is in EVIDENCE.md.

## Size and use

The model has 27.8 billion dense parameters, a 262,144-token context window, and accepts text and images as input while producing text. It runs on one GPU: about 52 GB in BF16, 29 GB in FP8 and 23 GB in NVFP4, the latter only on Blackwell GPUs. GGUF files are also available. Weights are published on Hugging Face and ModelScope.
